claims.text: In-situ high-temperature oxidation testing can reveal time-resolved details of oxide-scale formation in high-entropy alloys.
In-situ synchrotron X-ray or advanced electron microscopy can reveal oxide-scale spallation mechanisms.
Information obtained from in-situ oxidation testing can be leveraged to enhance oxidation resistance without relying solely on composition changes.
The proposed starting material is an as-cast and homogenized high-entropy or refractory alloy susceptible to elevated-temperature oxidation.
High-temperature diffraction can monitor oxide-scale evolution in real time during thermal exposure.
High-temperature microscopy can monitor oxide-scale evolution in real time during thermal exposure.
The relevant oxidation environment is approximately 800–1200 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere with controlled heating rates and dwell times.
Dynamic oxide-phase formation and transformation are structural mediators of high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Spallation behavior and elemental distribution at the alloy–oxide interface are observable structural mediators.
Time-resolved in-situ XRD can identify complex oxide phases and their time–temperature-dependent formation or transformation.
Time-resolved identification of oxide phases and spallation events enables process or composition parameters to be tailored to stabilize protective oxide scales.
Stabilizing a protective oxide scale increases oxidation resistance.
The proposed method will produce a more adherent and stable oxide scale with reduced mass gain and reduced spallation during long-term exposure.
A more adherent and stable oxide scale with reduced mass gain and spallation leads to enhanced oxidation resistance.
Conventional ex-situ oxidation testing supplies only post-exposure data and can miss transient stages of scale evolution.
Missing transient stages limits the accuracy of oxidation-resistance design strategies based only on ex-situ testing.
In-situ instrumentation may not yield a solution when oxide stability is controlled by factors beyond microstructural control, such as extremely aggressive environments.
The correlation between in-situ observations and extended high-temperature oxidation performance has not been fully quantified.
In CrMnFeCoNi, Mn is the major oxide-forming element in vacuum and air and forms non-protective oxides that deplete Mn from the bulk alloy.
In-situ observations should predict final microstructures or improve oxidation-resistance design strategies compared with ex-situ-only data.
